e.t: This word describes something that is “not burdensome”—something that does not weigh heavily on another person. It functions as a descriptive word, focusing on the absence of an unwanted load or demand. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 11:9. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: it does not impose a burden.

e.t: This word describes how a person conducts himself or lives, and in some contexts it refers to returning to a place. Its central idea is movement or behavior viewed as a person’s way of life: one may “live” in a certain manner, or “return” from one place to another. It occurs nine times in the Greek New Testament, including uses rendered “live” and “return.” The surrounding verse determines which sense is intended.

This word means “charcoal fire,” referring to a fire made with burning charcoal. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in John: John 18:18 and John 21:9. The word therefore identifies a specific kind of fire rather than fire in the broadest sense. The references establish its two uses, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular significance of each scene.

e.t: This verb means “to eject” or “to eject from,” describing the act of forcing someone or something out. It expresses removal rather than merely leaving voluntarily. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Acts 18:16. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the active removal or expulsion of someone from a place or situation.

This Greek New Testament word means “weak,” describing someone or something that lacks strength. It is used as a normal description rather than naming a particular person or object. The word appears 26 times in the Greek New Testament, across 24 verses, so its meaning is broad enough to apply wherever weakness is being described. The surrounding words determine whether the weakness concerns a person, a condition, or a situation. Its central idea remains a lack of strength. This word describes someone who is disorderly or idle—conduct that is not properly ordered or usefully engaged. It functions as a description of a person’s behavior rather than naming an object or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Thessalonians 5:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense points to conduct marked by disorder or idleness.

Bethphage is a proper place name, referring to a location mentioned in the New Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word or action, but as the name of a place. The name occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context, which is not included here.

Old age refers to the later stage of life, when a person has grown elderly. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Luke 1:36, and points to old age. Its basic meaning is age advanced by the passing of years; it identifies a person’s condition of being elderly rather than describing an action or event. The surrounding verse supplies the particular context, but the word itself centers on advanced age.

e.t: This word means “to kneel,” describing the physical act of lowering oneself onto one’s knees. It focuses on bodily posture rather than, by itself, explaining the reason or attitude behind that posture; the surrounding verse supplies that context. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, in four verses. Its uses appear in Matthew and Mark, showing a repeated description of someone adopting a kneeling position.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb describes loaning or receiving something temporarily—to lend or to borrow. Its central idea is an exchange in which one person provides something with the expectation that it will be returned, or seeks to receive it for a time. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, in three verses: once in Matthew and three times in Luke. The surrounding verse determines whether the action is viewed from the giver’s side, “lend,” or the receiver’s side, “borrow.”

e.t: This word means “to be scattered” or “to scatter,” describing people being spread out rather than remaining together. It functions as an action word and focuses on the movement or condition of being dispersed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Acts: Acts 8:1, Acts 8:4, and Acts 11:19. Its repeated use in these passages keeps the central idea consistent: people were separated and spread into different places. The surrounding verse and passage determine the particular circumstances of that scattering.

This word means “teaching” or “of teaching”—the communication of instruction or what is taught. It refers to teaching as a message, activity, or body of instruction, rather than to the teacher personally. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 30 times, showing that teaching is a recurring part of the biblical record. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and passage. [p03:word:greek-nt:G1322:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G1322:occurrences]

This word means “slavery,” referring to the condition or status of being enslaved. It describes slavery as a state rather than an action performed by someone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages in Romans, Galatians, and Hebrews. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains slavery or enslavement.

This word means “if indeed,” “if since,” or “if so,” and it connects a statement with a condition treated as real or strongly expected. It can also carry the sense “since,” presenting the condition as a basis for what follows. Thus, it is more than a bare question about possibility: it helps affirm or press the connection between two parts of an argument. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, all in six different verses.

e.t: This word means to be awe-struck—to be overwhelmed with wonder. It describes a powerful response that leaves a person astonished or deeply affected by what has been seen or experienced. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Mark’s Gospel. Its meaning points to more than ordinary surprise: it expresses a strong sense of amazement that can capture a person’s attention and shape the way he or she responds. The surrounding verse determines what specifically caused this wonder.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to choose” or “to select.” It describes deliberately picking one person or thing from among others, rather than merely noticing or encountering it. The word can function in statements about people being chosen, someone selecting a place, or a person being set apart by choice. It occurs 22 times in the Greek New Testament, so it expresses a recurring idea of intentional selection. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding passage says was chosen.

e.t: This word means to be astonished or amazed—an intense reaction of wonder or surprise. It describes people who are deeply affected by what they hear, see, or learn, so that ordinary expectations are interrupted. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 13 times, chiefly in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, and it can describe a response to teaching, remarkable works, or an unexpected truth. The word portrays a strong inward impression expressed as visible amazement, while the specific reason for that reaction depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word means “to draw” or “to drag,” describing the act of pulling something or someone from one place toward another. It can also express drawing a person toward something, including by persuasion, when the surrounding sentence gives that sense. Thus, its central idea is movement produced by pulling, whether the object is a net, a person, or another thing. It occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, with several uses in John and additional uses in Acts and James.

This Greek New Testament word means “goodwill”—a favorable desire, intention, or pleasure directed toward someone or something. It can describe what a person desires, what brings pleasure, or what is graciously purposed. Thus, its basic idea is not merely goodness in the abstract, but a benevolent disposition or a choice that reflects favor. The word occurs nine times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in passages from Matthew, Luke, Romans, Ephesians, Philippians, and 2 Thessalonians. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek New Testament word means “sound”—an audible noise or disturbance that can be heard. It is a noun, referring to what reaches the ear rather than to an action or spoken message itself. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, including descriptions of a sound heard by people and the sound associated with a significant heavenly or earthly event. Its exact force in any passage depends on what produces the sound and how the surrounding sentence describes it.

e.h: God and What Belongs to Him
e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “God” and can also express something about, by, of, or directed to God. It refers to God himself or identifies a relationship with him, depending on how it functions in a sentence. The word is very common, occurring 1,317 times in the Greek New Testament, so its exact English wording may change with context while its central reference remains God. It appears throughout the New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation.

Jordan is the name of a geographic place repeatedly mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It is rendered as “Jordan” and functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word. This word occurs 15 times in the Greek New Testament, across Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Its references include Matthew 3:5, Matthew 3:6, and John 10:40, showing that Jordan is a recurring location in the Gospel accounts.

e.t: This word means “to prepare”—to make something or someone ready for what is coming. It is a verb describing purposeful preparation rather than merely waiting. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times, including passages about preparing the way and making ready for a person or purpose. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being prepared and the surrounding context.

This Greek New Testament word means “sum” or “the point”—the main conclusion or central matter being stated. It can refer to what brings several matters together into one concise result, or to the chief point of an argument. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, appearing once in Acts and once in Hebrews. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic idea is the overall sum or central point.

Clement is a personal name, referring to an individual named Clement rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 4:3. The name itself does not explain the person’s role or character; those details must come from the surrounding passage. As a word, its meaning is simply the person’s name, rendered consistently as “Clement.”

This word means “to swim,” describing the action of moving through water by swimming. It is a verb, so it expresses an activity rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:43. The word’s basic meaning is direct and specific; its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the situation being described.

This word means “lion,” referring to the animal. In the Greek New Testament, it appears nine times across nine verses, including both singular and plural renderings. It functions as a noun naming one lion or more than one. The word occurs most often in Revelation, but its central meaning remains consistent: lion. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

e.t: This word means “to be drunk” or “to get drunk.” It describes becoming intoxicated or being in a drunken condition. In the Greek New Testament, it is used six times, each in a different verse, including passages that speak about drinking, drunkenness, and people perceived as drunk. The word describes a condition caused by drink rather than simply mentioning the act of drinking. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

e.t: This word means “to imitate”—to follow another person’s example by doing what they do. It describes adopting a pattern of conduct, whether that pattern is worthy of following or not. In the New Testament, it occurs four times, including instructions connected with faithful leaders and warnings about following evil rather than good. Its basic focus is active likeness: a person’s actions reflect the example they have chosen to follow.

e.t: Naphtali is a proper name, used to identify Naphtali rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, in Matthew and Revelation. Its ordinary meaning remains the name itself; the surrounding verse determines what is being said about Naphtali in each occurrence. The name is rendered “Naphtali” in the available English renderings.

This word means “completeness” or “wholeness.” It describes a condition of being complete, whole, or lacking nothing essential. As a noun, it names that state rather than describing an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 3:16. The surrounding verse and passage determine how this idea is applied there, but the word itself points to completeness or restored wholeness rather than partialness or deficiency.

Urbanus is a personal name, not a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Romans 16:9. The available rendering preserves the name as “Urbanus,” so the word functions as an identifying name rather than a general term with a broader stated definition. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word describes craftiness or cunning—the use of clever, often deceptive methods to achieve an aim. It points to shrewdness that can mislead others rather than straightforward wisdom or honest skill. In the Greek New Testament, it appears five times, consistently translated as “craftiness” and once as “cunning.” Its use spans warnings about deception, hidden motives, and methods that can lead people away from what is true. The surrounding passage determines the precise way this craftiness is operating in a particular verse.

e.t: This word means “on the other side” or refers to the “other side” of a place or boundary. It describes location, distinguishing one side from another rather than naming a specific object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 23 times, so it is a recurring way of indicating where someone or something is in relation to another place. Its exact force—such as across a body of water or beyond a region—comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “pure,” describing something regarded as clean, genuine, or free from mixture. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, appearing once in Mark and once in John. Its repeated rendering as “pure” confirms this central sense. The word’s precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the substance or thing being discussed.

This word means “traitor”: a person who betrays someone who should receive loyalty or trust. It describes a betrayer rather than merely someone who disagrees or turns away. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Luke 6:16, Acts 7:52, and 2 Timothy 3:4. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains betrayal and disloyalty.

e.t: This word means “to be united to” or “to join,” describing being attached or united with another. It appears twice in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 10:7 and Ephesians 5:31. In both places, it expresses a joining that establishes close union rather than a casual meeting. The word therefore points to attachment and unity, especially when one person is joined to another. Its precise emphasis in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is to join closely or become united.

Rhegium is the name rendered “Rhegium,” functioning as a proper place-name rather than a term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 28:13. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, no further lesson or contextual detail should be attached to it. Its meaning is therefore simply the geographic name Rhegium.

“Sadducee” refers to a member of the Sadducees, a group named in the Greek New Testament. The word functions as a group designation rather than a description of an action or quality. It appears 14 times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Acts. The plural “Sadducees” refers to the group collectively. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This word describes earnest diligence—acting with devoted care, energy, and urgency rather than laziness or delay. It can also refer to hurry or prompt action, so its emphasis is on giving something serious, energetic attention. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times across 12 verses, including uses connected with serving, responding, and acting promptly. The central idea is active earnestness: a person does not merely intend to act but applies himself or herself with determined care.

This word means “sparrow,” referring to a small bird. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times and is rendered “sparrows.” Its references occur in Matthew 10 and Luke 12, where the word is used in statements about these birds. The word itself identifies the bird; the surrounding verse supplies the fuller point being made about it. Thus, its ordinary meaning is simply a sparrow or sparrows, depending on the sentence.

e.t: This word means “to discuss” or “to discuss together.” It describes people talking over a matter with one another, rather than merely speaking a single word or making an isolated statement. As a verb, it expresses the action of considering or debating something jointly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 20:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is shared discussion about a matter under consideration.

e.t: This word means to agree to something or approve of it. It describes willing assent: a person accepts a matter, supports it, or joins in approving what is being done. The sense can apply to approval of another person’s action as well as agreement to a request or arrangement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, so its basic idea remains consistent while its precise force is shaped by each sentence’s surrounding context.

The word “tetrarch” refers to a ruler who bears that title. It functions as a designation for a person’s governing position, rather than as a personal name. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times: once in Matthew, twice in Luke, and once in Acts. Each occurrence is rendered “tetrarch,” so the central meaning remains consistent across these passages. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the particular tetrarch being mentioned and the role he has in that passage.

Punishment refers to a penalty imposed because of wrongdoing. This word names the consequence assigned to someone who has done wrong, focusing on the punishment itself rather than the action that brought it about. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Hebrews 10:29, and is rendered “punishment.” Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the penalty imposed for wrongdoing.

e.t: This word means “to shudder”—to react with a sudden involuntary tremor. It describes a bodily response rather than a spoken statement or deliberate action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 2:19, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The precise force in that verse belongs to its surrounding context.

This word means “arrogance”: an inflated sense of one’s own importance that expresses proud self-assertion rather than humility. It describes a person’s boastful attitude or behavior, especially when self-importance shapes how that person treats others. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 12:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the proud elevation of oneself above others.

This word means “to roar,” describing a loud, forceful cry. It functions as an action word, portraying someone or something making a powerful roaring sound rather than merely being noisy or speaking. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 5:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of roaring—an intense sound meant to be heard. This is a vivid word for loud, threatening-sounding vocal expression.
